item.title: Protesters in Indonesia Demand Action to Stop Fires in Rainforests
item.description:
Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets this week in Indonesia to voice anger at what they see as their government’s failure to stop fires in rainforests that have blanketed their country in a sickening haze.

The demonstrations by students and members of civil society groups began on Monday and spread to more than a half dozen cities across the country including on the island of Borneo, where many of the fires are burning.

These are the latest in a series of protests that have been building since August, in which participants have demanded that the nation’s president, Prabowo Subianto, declare a national emergency and take steps to prevent destructive agricultural practices that many blame for fueling the blazes.

“I have the right to breathe,” read one banner at a rally in the Indonesian capital, Jakarta. “Extinguish the fires immediately!”

“The situation has reached a level that is completely, utterly abnormal,” said one protester, Naomi Artika, a law student at the University of Palangka Raya in Central Kalimantan, a province on Borneo.

Government leaders defended their response, which has not been able to halt the fires.

“We are all trying our best,” the state secretary, Prasetyo Hadi, said on Tuesday, according to local media. “We have deployed ground troops, aircraft and volunteers to put out the fires.”

While fires appear every year during the dry season that begins in April, this year’s are the worst on record. Earlier this year, there was less rain during the usually wet months that precede April, which experts blamed on both global warming and an El Niño climate shift.

The size of the fires remains contested. In its last tally made in July, the Indonesian government said about 780 square miles had burned this year — twice the land area of New York City. But Nusantara Atlas, an open-access platform that tracks deforestation globally, estimates the amount of forest destroyed is closer to 7,400 square miles.

The smoke has spread into neighboring Malaysia and Singapore, which have also reacted angrily, blaming Indonesia for not doing enough to contain the blazes.

Within Indonesia, the smoke from the burning rainforests has created a growing health crisis that has closed schools, caused widespread breathing disorders and forced many to stay indoors.

According to the Health Ministry, more than 306,309 residents of Indonesia’s seven provinces most heavily affected by the smoke have suffered acute respiratory illnesses over the last two months. Nearly half of those — 146,037 cases — were children under the age of 10, the ministry said on Sunday.

Some medical experts say the figures undercount the actual number of people falling sick.

“Lately, we’ve been seeing more scans showing signs of pneumonia, particularly among children and the elderly,” said Sigit Riatno, a radiologist in Kandangan, a town in South Kalimantan on Borneo. Of the roughly 60 chest X-rays he examines each day, about a third now show evidence of respiratory problems. “This situation is really worrying.”

One of those forced to stay indoors is Davankan Khalid Bhumi, a 2-year-old who has been unable to leave his home in Pontianak, the capital of West Kalimantan Province on Borneo, to meet playmates or swim. The haze outside is just too thick for little Khalid, who has been sensitive to smoke since infancy and needs a respiratory device called a nebulizer three times a week to help him sleep, said his mother, Era Oktafiansyah.

“It breaks my heart to hear his ‘ngiik ngiik’ breath and coughing,” said Ms. Era, 30, using a word that describes the wheezing sound her son makes.

Indonesia’s burning rainforests are often pointed to as a symptom of an ailing planet, an environmental disruption on par with the deforestation of the Amazon. The fires are widely blamed on “slash-and-burn” clearing of rainforest for agriculture to grow cash crops including palm oil and timber. The flames jump to nearby areas of peat, a type of wetland made up of decaying plant matter that extends deep beneath the forest floor but that has dried out.

Once ignited, the peat can smolder out of control for weeks or even months.

Mr. Prabowo has ordered additional resources to reinforce firefighting operations across the country, calling it “a top priority for us.” At the same time, he has resisted declaring the fires a natural disaster, which would compel his government to take more action.

“Ultimately, the only real solution is rain,” he said last week.

His government has pursued other policies, including energy self-sufficiency, that opponents say are having an adverse impact on the rainforests.

The president’s special envoy for climate and energy has proposed using 49,000 square miles of degraded forest as feedstock for biofuel production. He said the plan wouldn’t cut down old-growth forest, but critics say it will still damage the overall ecosystem, leaving it more vulnerable to fires.

This week’s protests were also held on the second anniversary of the presidency of Mr. Prabowo, whom the demonstrators criticized for what they saw as a lack of action. “If we burn, you burn with us!” one banner said in Jakarta.

Last month, Nafas Kalbar, a coalition of civil society groups in West Kalimantan, filed a class-action lawsuit accusing the government of negligence in its failure to stop the blazes or to take preventive measures against the El Niño, which was foreseeable.

“Clean air and clean water are fundamental human rights,” said Glorio Sanen, the coalition’s lawyer.

In Malaysia, a former health minister, Khairy Jamaluddin, urged his government to push Indonesia to take action. “When somebody else is choking you, you don’t allow them to continue to choke you,” he said in a podcast.

Singapore’s prime minister, Lawrence Wong, said his country would punish private companies blamed for the destructive agricultural practices that cause the fires.

Dr. Sigit, the radiologist, says the prolonged haze will have health impacts reaching beyond even the proliferation of breathing ailments that he has observed. Many may suffer from chronic respiratory problems that will impose a long-term burden on their lives as well as on hospitals and Indonesia’s national health insurance program, whose budget is already strained.

“The impact of smog on health, especially the respiratory tract and lungs, will incur even greater costs,” he said.

Ms. Era, the mother of Khalid, looks forward to a day when the air is clean enough to allow her son to play outside again. In the meantime, she has closed gaps and openings around their home to stop the smoke from entering.

“We do stay indoors, but how do you keep a child from breathing?” she said.

item.title: The Epstein Files Produce an Unlikely Weapon for the Houthi Messaging Wars
item.description:
The Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen is not only firing missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia, but also waging a propaganda war against the kingdom on social media.

A key character in the group’s communications campaign is, oddly, Jeffrey Epstein, the deceased American sex offender, some of whose files the U.S. Department of Justice has released.

The Houthis have recently homed in on a particular set of revelations to try to undermine Saudi Arabia’s leaders — namely, reports showing that associates of the Saudi royal court sent tapestries that had draped the holiest site in Islam to Mr. Epstein’s private island.

The Houthis control much of Yemen. Their communications show a profound awareness of news that their sworn enemies generate. They are willing to deploy the information in many forms — songs, videos, speeches, statements, influencer posts and more — to build support and target foes, including Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognized Yemeni government they are fighting. They portray themselves as defenders of Islam against corrupt foreign influences.

Now, the group has stepped up its messaging efforts, after Yemen’s civil war reignited this summer amid the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

The Saudis last month accused the Houthis of firing a drone at the Muslim holy city of Mecca, saying the attack was a “disgraceful” act that intended to provoke Muslims. The Houthis denied the accusation.

Rallying their expansive network to try to turn the accusation of religious betrayal against the kingdom, the Houthis pointed to the reports that Mr. Epstein had received tapestries that had draped the Kaba, the cubed building in Mecca that is the spiritual center of Islam.

“Those who gave Epstein the Kaba’s cover are the ones targeting Mecca,” Mahdi al-Mashat, the Houthi president, said in a statement to the group’s official news media.

Saudi officials have not responded to the Houthi accusations about Mr. Epstein or the reports about the tapestries after new Justice Department files were released this year.

Variations on Mr. al-Mashat’s message were echoed across the Houthi network, including video commentary from a Yemeni comedian with more than 270,000 followers on X and a song by a traditional musician in Yemen.

“They are very plugged in,” said Mohammed al-Basha, founder of the risk advisory firm Basha Report and a Yemen analyst in Washington who has tracked the evolution of Houthi communications over more than 20 years.

The group’s messaging operations have morphed from essentially “a two-man crew,” Mr. al-Basha said, to an organized media system. It spans television channels, websites, radio, newspapers, email campaigns and official and unofficial social media accounts. There is also a brigade of cultural influencers — a support network involving people who are ideologically aligned with the group and other Iranian proxies but not necessarily paid — who amplify a range of content in line with their ideology.

Like other groups in Iran’s “axis of resistance,” the Houthis are “obsessed” with Mr. Epstein, said Mr. al-Basha. The disgraced financier, he added, serves as shorthand for the corruption of the United States and Israel and is invoked to bolster antisemitic conspiracy theories that Jews and Zionists run the world.

A secular American Jew who officials said killed himself in a New York jail in 2019 while facing criminal charges on the trafficking of underage girls, Mr. Epstein frequently features in speeches by the Houthis’ leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi. He mentioned Mr. Epstein in a speech this month celebrating the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel that sparked the Gaza war and in another in September about the Houthis’ 2014 takeover of the Yemeni capital, Sanaa.

“Epstein’s files demand serious attention,” Mr. al-Houthi said in a February address. “They unveil a Zionist incubator that trains leaders and elites.”

The Houthis have positioned their fight with Saudi Arabia as part of the broader war the Iranian axis says it is waging against the United States and the “Epstein class,” including Saudi leaders, said Moustafa Ayad, who leads research at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue in London on Islamist movements’ online ecosystems.

The Houthi motto calls for death to America and Israel. Connecting the rulers of Saudi Arabia — the birthplace of Islam — to these core enemies reinforce’s the group’s stance that, although the Saudis have no diplomatic relations with Israel, they are “one block” with the United States, Mr. Ayad said. U.S. weapons and military support were essential to the yearslong bloody bombing campaign that Saudi Arabia waged against the Houthis.

The Saudi-backed Yemeni government has its own approach to propaganda, though it does not have the same unity of messaging, Mr. al-Basha said, because its Presidential Leadership Council is made up of leaders with various ideologies and affiliations to different military groups. They are unified in their opposition to the Houthis, but “there is no one voice for these groups,” he added.

The Houthis’ messaging to the Arab world has been prolific, and their content went truly global after they targeted commercial ships in the Red Sea in 2023 in alliance with Hamas during the Gaza war. Since July, as fighting with Saudi Arabia has reignited, the group has turned back to their own conflict and shifted their messaging accordingly.

“Now, they are very specifically singling out Saudi Arabia” and “almost laser-focused on decimating” the standing of the kingdom’s de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said Mr. Ayad.

The Yemeni comedian Mustafa Al-Moumr was previously critical of and jailed by the Houthis, but since his release in 2023 he has aligned his content with the group’s talking points. It is not clear what is behind his new work, or whether he is operating under duress.

In the current conflict, he has produced a stream of content critical of the kingdom and Prince Mohammed, including music videos, commentary and short dramas. One music video posted in July shows him as the Saudi crown prince singing about his fear of the Houthis while aides report militia attacks, and ends with the royal captured in his palace at gunpoint. The post has had more than 300,000 views.

Another major theme in Houthi content is the toll of Saudi Arabia’s intervention in Yemen. A Saudi-led bombing campaign in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which began in 2015, precipitated one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises and contributed to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people in Yemen from violence, hunger and disease.

When Saudi Arabia’s foreign minister, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, was filmed last month in New York being berated by an activist in Arabic, a Houthi spokesman, Ameel Hayyan, posted the clip on social media, writing that Saudi Arabia is loathed globally “due to its crimes against Muslims and especially the savage massacres it committed in Yemen.”

Since the civil war in Yemen reignited in August, some 260,000 people have been displaced, according to the United Nations. Nearly 1,600 people have been killed, the World Health Organization said this week. And the Houthis have been pummeling Saudi Arabia’s aviation and energy infrastructure for weeks, killing at least 22 civilians.

Some of the content has emerged in the recent conflict is “essentially a mimicking of the Iranian approach” to propaganda, Mr. Ayad said.

Since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February, Iran has been adept at reaching an international audience on the messaging front.

Explosive Media, an Iranian group that has produced viral Lego videos, last month created “a Lego retelling of Yemen’s battles and victories,” a fantastical take on Houthi fighting with Saudi Arabia that shows the militia storming a Saudi military base with a golden statue of Mr. Trump and ends with a Houthi commander sipping from a mug marked “mocha,” alluding to their capture of the Red Sea port of Mokha, a gateways of early coffee trade.

The narratives are traveling far and wide, reaching seemingly unlikely sympathizers, at least some of whom share an obsession with conspiracy theories and Mr. Epstein.

Jake Shields, a retired mixed martial arts champion and popular right-wing podcaster and influencer, whom the Southern Poverty Law Center has accused of promoting “antisemitism, racism and bigotry,” posts about the Epstein files regularly. On a recent episode of his show, he spoke about the fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, expressing admiration for the militia’s resilience.

“I’m a big fan,” he said of the Houthis. “I think they’re kind of badass.”

It was precisely the kind of reputation and response that experts say the Houthis have sought to cultivate with their military and messaging campaigns.

James McManagan contributed reporting.

item.title: Brazil’s Most Divided Town Shows the Nation’s Shift to the Right
item.description:
It felt like doomsday for the Brazilian left. On Oct. 4, Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-wing presidential candidate, outperformed polls and edged ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a leftist.

The narrow margin was not enough to avoid a runoff on Sunday between the two candidates, but it was plenty to set off hand-wringing and soul-searching across progressive bubbles in big cities like São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, and a reorganization in Mr. Lula’s campaign.

A visit to Nanuque, a cattle-raising, churchgoing town 500 miles north of Rio de Janeiro, where crowds turn out on foot for an annual march for Jesus and on horseback for the nation’s independence day, offers clues to Mr. Lula’s lackluster showing and Mr. Bolsonaro’s rise.

The town of 35,000 sits in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais, which has backed the winner in every presidential election since 1988, when democracy returned to Brazil after a military dictatorship.

Atlantic

Ocean

Amazon R.

BRAZIL

MINAS GERAIS

BOLIVIA

Nanuque

São Paulo

Rio de Janeiro

ARGENTINA

500 miles

The New York Times

In the 2022 race, Nanuque, pronounced nah-NEW-key, was the most closely divided of Brazil’s 5,569 municipalities, with Mr. Bolsonaro’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, winning by one vote. (Jair Bolsonaro lost that election to Mr. Lula and was convicted of plotting a coup after trying to hold onto power.)

In 2026’s first round, the younger Bolsonaro finished ahead by two percentage points, the same margin he claimed in Brazil as a whole.

Mr. Bolsonaro’s ability to win similar towns — rooted in agriculture and with a strong Evangelical Christian presence — contributed to his strong first round showing.

He won 79 percent of towns with a large agricultural sector, a high percentage of evangelical Christians and that have less than 50,000 residents, according to an analysis by Marco Faganello, a political data scientist at Fundação Getulio Vargas, a Brazilian university. Jair Bolsonaro won 53 percent of such towns in 2022’s first round.

In interviews with scores of voters in Nanuque, including truck drivers, cattle ranchers, farmworkers, business leaders and civil servants, those who have abandoned Mr. Lula cited unfulfilled economic promises, his past corruption scandals and their frustration with health care, among other reasons.

While many on the left remain staunch supporters of Mr. Lula, others who had voted for him before expressed fatigue over an 80-year-old incumbent running for a fourth term. His Workers’ Party has been in power for 18 of the last 24 years.

Valdirene Santos Moura, a cook who has voted for Mr. Lula before, acknowledged his accomplishments, including introducing programs that helped the poor. But now, she said, she was “tired of him already.”

Geremias Alves de Souza, a coffee picker, dropped his voice so his wife would not hear him say he was voting for Mr. Bolsonaro. He said he associates the younger Mr. Bolsonaro with his father’s tough on crime policies.

Other voters said their support for Mr. Bolsonaro was based not on his track record — which they said they were unfamiliar with — but on their affection for Jair Bolsonaro.

Some said they were simply fed up with politics and were planning to abstain on Sunday.

One is Jovenildo Carvalho, 45, who runs a start-up that uses drones to deploy wasps to attack caterpillars that ravage sugar cane fields.

Mr. Carvalho, who grew up with no electricity and wore Che Guevara T-shirts in college, said he has no faith in either candidate’s ability to lead the country, and was frustrated by Brazil’s deeply polarized political landscape.

“I’d like to see Brazil without the veil of fanaticism and blind passion that it has today,” he said.

Agribusiness in Brazil, which includes farming, cattle ranching, meatpacking plants and ethanol distilleries, has become a behemoth, accounting for a quarter of the country’s economy. For the first time, Brazil may soon surpass the United States in agricultural exports.

The sector’s leaders are among Mr. Lula’s biggest detractors, criticizing him over high interest rates, environmental regulations and gas subsidies that have reduced ethanol demand during the Iran war.

“If it were Lula against a stray dog, everyone would vote for the stray dog,” said Luiz Daniel Silva Rocha, whose family owns DASA, a large sugar mill and ethanol distillery outside Nanuque that employs hundreds of people.

The biggest target for local business leaders is Mr. Lula’s signature welfare program, known as Bolsa Família, which provides cash transfers to low income families. Brazilians agree that it has helped pull millions out of extreme poverty, but some now consider it a handout to those who aren’t financially desperate.

“In Brazil today, the policy is to reward those who don’t work,” said Ângelo Márcio Sousa Silva, DASA’s general manager.

Nearly 3,000 families in Nanuque receive cash transfers, according to government data, and business leaders say it has made it hard for them to fill jobs. Between DASA and the town’s largest employer, a meatpacking plant, there are about 120 full-time vacancies, leaving the plants operating below capacity.

The Bolsa Família program came up repeatedly as a driving force behind people’s votes for both candidates, far more than topics that dominate election talk among urban elites, like a scandal roiling Brazil’s Supreme Court or worries about U.S. interference in Latin American elections.

People who work in the informal sector — as day laborers on farms or cleaning houses — but still receive cash benefits remain loyal to Mr. Lula.

Letícia Silva de Almeida, 33, is among those. She works seasonally helping harvest coffee and earns $24 per day. She also receives $150 a month through the cash transfer program, even though she said that money was not essential.

“If they cut it off today, I’d be OK,” she said.

That mind-set infuriates others. Tatiane Souza da Silva, a housekeeper, said friends urged her to understate her income to qualify for the cash program, but she has refused on principle.

“I see young women in good health — men too — refusing to work,” she said. “That ends up hurting the economy.” Once a Lula voter, she plans to vote for Mr. Bolsonaro on Sunday.

Mr. Lula has called Brazil’s free public health system “one of the masterpieces of health care worldwide.’’

That is not a word many in Nanuque would use. Many complained of long waits for specialists in faraway cities, even though a year ago, Mr. Lula launched a program meant to help underserved towns called “Now There Are Specialists.”

“We need the politicians to see us, when it comes to health care,” said Ana Paula Rodrigues dos Santos, 41, who was shopping for the lunches she cooks and sells for $6 each to make a living.

She said she needs her gall bladder removed but explained that the town’s public hospital lacks an intensive care unit, which her doctors have told her she may need since her obesity increases the risk of complications.

She has been on a waiting list at a hospital in a city three hours away for nearly three years, she said.

Ms. dos Santos described herself as an independent who was leaning toward Mr. Bolsonaro.

“It’s been going left, left, left and the left didn’t do anything for Brazil,” she said. “We have to put in new people.”

The right’s increased appeal among voters is not just fueled by growing frustration with Mr. Lula. It is also driven by religion. The percentage of Brazil’s population that is evangelical Christian has tripled since 1991, and members of Evangelical congregations lean heavily conservative.

Dozens of Evangelical churches dot rich and poor neighborhoods in Nanuque, where some pastors preach opposition to abortion and homosexuality.

At New Life Evangelical Church, a relatively wealthy congregation, the pastor, Bishop Robson Merry Teixeira Farias, said he believed nearly all of his 300 members would support Mr. Bolsonaro for president.

Even within less well off congregations, support for Mr. Bolsonaro was still strong, according to pastors and members.

Under Brazilian law, religious leaders cannot make endorsements from the pulpit, but Bishop Merry, as he is known, suggested that preferences can be telegraphed by promoting conservative values that align with specific candidates.

“We do not champion men, we champion causes,” he said.

In a town with no mall or cinema, churches are central to social life, and congregants arrive well dressed and as eager to socialize as to pray.

On Sunday, after church services, they will have a second chance to socialize — at Nanuque’s 21 polling stations.

“As the election approaches, it is the responsibility of leaders” like him, Bishop Merry said, “to pass along their vision.”

“The sheep always try to imitate the pastor,” he added.

Silvia Ribeiro contributed reporting from Rio de Janeiro.

item.title: How Long Will Russians Put Up With War? Here’s What They Told Us.
item.description:
I always get the same question when I return from reporting in Russia: When will Russians finally be fed up with the war?

They might seem to have good reason now. The war, for years mostly background noise among many Russians, feels more present. The economy is limping. Drivers have to wait in line for gas. Warehouses and data centers are going up in flames. Even Moscow at times comes under heavy attack, as it did on Thursday, when Ukraine launched 630 drones into the region.

One recent morning, I set out to ask Russians what they thought about all this. I went to Sofino, a town about an hour from Moscow, where Ukrainian drones a few days before had struck an industrial area, igniting a fire, and a residential complex, killing two people.

On the way, I pulled over at a Rosneft gas station where waiting cars snaked well past the exit lane. It had no diesel, but gasoline was available for about $3.25 a gallon — a steep price in Russia. A young man named Danya told me he had waited 30 minutes for gas.

He shrugged it off, repeating a refrain I hear all the time from Russians. “Everything is fine,” said Danya, who, like others I spoke with, asked that his last name not be used to avoid trouble with the authorities. He added that fuel shortages were overblown.

The war, he insisted, “doesn’t affect my life at all.”

“Everything is fine,” he said again.

Russians shrug for several reasons. They are silenced by the fear and conformity bred by a repressive government. They feel they have as much influence over their country’s politics as they do the weather. They are used to deprivation from centuries of political and economic crises. They keep their focus, as a coping mechanism, on what hasn’t changed. And they are flooded with anti-Ukraine propaganda from the state.

There is also a more fundamental explanation. Ukraine’s strategy, as it holds Russia to a near deadlock on the front lines, is to make Russians feel the war and demand an end. That includes the strikes on oil refineries that President Trump has pressured Ukraine to stop in recent days as he has openly favored President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

Although the Ukrainian campaign has significantly cut Russian oil production, causing clear economic damage, it has not been enough yet to drastically change life in Russia. Kyiv lacks the ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones that Russia fires at Ukrainian cities every day. And Ukraine’s strikes, focused mostly on economic and military targets, do not instill the same fear as Russia’s systematic assaults on Ukrainian civilian targets.

Ukraine’s attacks have politicized some Russians who before now had tried to ignore the war. People have rallied around the flag. In Sofino, outside an apartment building with a gaping hole in the third and fourth floors after the Ukrainian strike, I asked three warehouse workers if they felt angry at the Russian state for starting the war and letting it drag on for nearly five years.

“Quite the opposite, the attacks make people hate them even more, because their homes have been damaged,” one young man said, referring to Ukrainians and their Western backers. He asked that his name be withheld.

Inside the building, a woman named Lusya was dragging a trash bag down the rubble-strewn stairs. She said it was surreal watching television that evening because there was no mention of the attack that had suddenly rendered her homeless. Still, she said she trusted Russia’s leaders.

“I support my president, even more so after all this, because you realize you just have to support the man and consolidate around him,” she said.

“I believe we are very lucky to have Putin,” she added.

Enduring adversity is a source of national pride for Russians. Successive generations have heard tales of the sacrifices of World War II. Waiting in line for basic goods was common during the Soviet era. The war in Ukraine, for many, is just another hardship to bear.

“People get used to a ‘new normal’ again and again,” said Elena Stein of the Berlin-based Center for Independent Social Research, which supports research inside Russia.

Many Russians are just tuning out the war. In a poll last month by the independent Levada Center, nearly 60 percent of respondents said they paid little or no attention to the fighting, the highest level ever recorded. Six in 10 said the country was on the right track, up 10 percentage points from the level in June, just after an earlier drone attack on Moscow.

The reliability of polling data is limited in autocratic Russia. But such numbers indicate that Mr. Putin’s yearslong effort to insulate Russians enough from the war that he can conduct it unimpeded is still largely working, despite mounting challenges.

“The pressure and the problems that are there are, in my view, not intense enough for him to reconsider at this point,” said Janis Kluge, a Russia analyst at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs.

Other analysts have said that the Trump administration’s recent decisions to engage in business deals with the Kremlin while demanding no concessions will only harden Mr. Putin’s resolve to continue fighting until he achieves his objectives in Ukraine.

While polls show that growing numbers of Russians want the war to be over, the vast majority say it should end only on Russia’s terms. Many appear ready to continue deferring to Mr. Putin.

Kirill, 36, a choreographer with a small hoop earring, said that aside from the price of gas, “I don’t feel it at all.”

“I’m not going to complain, because I know that this is my country, I’m going to support it no matter what,” he said. “I know that the people at the top can clearly see the bigger picture.”

As I spoke with Kirill and others at the Rosneft station, the store’s manager, Irina, came to admonish me for interviewing her customers. But soon she was sharing her own story.

Unlike the people in line, Irina did not deny the war’s role in her life.

She said she had told her 11-year-old daughter that if a drone or missile struck the gas station, she risked dying on the spot. Her mother-in-law works as a security guard at a warehouse complex that has been struck. And her brother has been fighting on the front since 2022. She said it was a miracle that he remained alive, adding that he had survived nights when up to 40 people were killed. He told her that he expected the war to continue until 2030.

She voiced the trademark sense of fatalism in Russia. “We’ll just have to endure it,” she said. “If we die, we die. I’ve already made peace with it.”

Irina was not as inclined as others to defer to the government’s approach on the war. She said she felt that officials were not telling the truth about casualties on the battlefield and in long-range strikes on Russian cities.

Eventually, this sort of mistrust, coupled with a worsening economic outlook, could set off more expressions of dissatisfaction, said Jeremy Morris, a sociologist at the University of Aarhus in Denmark who conducts fieldwork in Russia.

While it might not happen soon, he said, most Russians are not apathetic and apolitical, as they are sometimes portrayed. They just lack outlets for action as the government has grown more repressive.

During parliamentary elections last month, I visited the headquarters of Yabloko, Russia’s main antiwar party. I spoke with Maria, 24, one of the approximately 20 percent of Russians who tell pollsters they oppose the war.

She expressed indignation as she described reading English-language posts on social media describing Russians as a “slave nation.” She pointed to comments like one recently by a European Union spokeswoman, who said that “if Russian citizens face the consequences of this war, they have a chance domestically to take action against it.”

Maria described the costs of speaking up in Russia, where 1,856 people are currently incarcerated as political prisoners, according to the banned human rights group Memorial.

“None of you have gone through the experience of the average person living under totalitarianism, repression, total fear and the absence of free speech,” she said. “You can’t demand that we go on strike or turn out for protests, because all we’ll achieve is ending up in prison — or getting killed.”

item.title: Palestinian Gunmen Open Fire on Israelis in the West Bank, Officials Say
item.description:
Palestinian gunmen opened fire on Israelis in the West Bank on Friday, the Israeli military said, just four days before national elections and against the backdrop of a broader uptick in violence in the occupied territory.

Five people were wounded in the attack, near the city of Hebron, including two who were in critical condition, according to Magen David Adom, Israel’s ambulance service. The Israeli military said its soldiers had killed two assailants.

Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, the Israeli military’s chief of staff, said that “the troops’ swift action prevented an even more serious attack and further harm to civilians and security forces.” A large amount of ammunition was found in a vehicle used by the attackers, the military said.

Hours after the shooting, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel ordered security forces to cordon off Hebron, the most populous city in the West Bank, and to prepare for a “lockdown” of the territory starting on Friday. He added that security forces were conducting extensive arrests.

Soldiers and police officers have launched “offensive counterterrorism operations in the Hebron area,” the military said. It added that soldiers were operating in the homes of the assailants and other suspects.

Violence has escalated in the West Bank since the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the subsequent war in Gaza. Israeli forces have conducted sweeping military raids, saying they are seeking to root out Palestinian armed groups, displacing tens of thousands of people.

Palestinian gunmen have conducted shootings and stabbings against Israel civilians and soldiers. Last month, an Israeli man was shot and killed in the central West Bank, according to Israeli authorities, who said they had detained a Palestinian suspect over the attack.

Extremist settlers have carried out attacks on Palestinians, setting mosques and homes ablaze, stealing livestock and cutting down olive trees. That aggression has forced entire Palestinian communities to flee.

Settler attacks against Palestinians have escalated in recent weeks during the annual olive harvest, which is a cultural touchstone for Palestinians and an economic lifeline for many families.

Hamas praised the attack on Friday as a “heroic operation,” but it stopped short of taking credit.

The militant group also called on Palestinians bearing weapons to shoot “bullets at the chest of the occupiers, their soldiers and their criminal settlers.”

Yousef Jabari, the mayor of Hebron, said the Israeli authorities had closed off every way in and out of Hebron and shut down the Palestinian-run part of the Ibrahimi Mosque, a shrine in the city revered by Jews, Muslims and Christians as the burial place of Abraham. Jews refer to the Ibrahimi Mosque as the Tomb of Patriarchs.

“This is collective punishment against innocent people,” Mr. Jabari said in an interview. “Why should the entire city be besieged? Why should people with health appointments or social events in other cities be forced to stay home?”

Aaron Boxerman contributed reporting.
